reference.source: Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Type 1 (hepatorenal) is the most severe form and stems from deficiency of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase in the tyrosine degradation pathway
Acute infantile presentation features liver failure, coagulopathy, ascites and a cabbage-like or boiled-cabbage odour
Chronic disease produces cirrhosis, renal tubular dysfunction with hypophosphataemic rickets (renal Fanconi syndrome), and a very high risk of hepatocellular carcinoma
Painful neurological crises resembling acute porphyria can occur due to accumulated succinylacetone inhibiting porphyrin synthesis
Succinylacetone in blood or urine is the key diagnostic marker and is now used in newborn screening
Type 2 causes eye and skin lesions with keratitis, and type 3 is a rare neurological form
Management is centred on nitisinone (NTBC), which blocks tyrosine degradation upstream, combined with dietary restriction of phenylalanine and tyrosine
Nitisinone therapy has transformed outcomes and reduced the need for liver transplantation, though HCC surveillance is still required
reference.pathophysiology: Hereditary tyrosinemia type 1 is an autosomal recessive defect of fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase, the final enzyme of tyrosine catabolism. Its deficiency causes accumulation of the upstream intermediates maleylacetoacetate and fumarylacetoacetate, which are converted to the toxic metabolites succinylacetone and succinylacetoacetate. These compounds are highly reactive and injure hepatocytes and renal tubular cells, driving hepatic failure, cirrhosis, malignant transformation and renal Fanconi syndrome. Succinylacetone also inhibits delta-aminolaevulinic acid dehydratase, causing porphyrin precursor accumulation and porphyria-like neurological crises. Nitisinone works by inhibiting 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate dioxygenase upstream, preventing formation of the toxic distal metabolites.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal hepatitis and other causes of infantile liver failure
Other causes of renal Fanconi syndrome (cystinosis, Lowe syndrome)
Acute intermittent porphyria (for the neurological crises)
additionalInvestigations: Plasma amino acids showing elevated tyrosine (and often methionine)
Liver function tests, coagulation profile and alpha-fetoprotein (markedly raised, and a tumour marker)
Renal tubular studies for Fanconi syndrome and assessment for rickets
Liver imaging and AFP for hepatocellular carcinoma surveillance; FAH molecular testing
redFlags: Acute liver failure with coagulopathy in an infant is a metabolic emergency
Porphyria-like neurological crises with pain, weakness and possible respiratory compromise
Rising or persistently elevated alpha-fetoprotein or hepatic nodules suggesting hepatocellular carcinoma
Severe electrolyte and phosphate loss from renal tubulopathy
reference.prognosis: Untreated type 1 disease historically carried a poor prognosis with death from liver failure in infancy or later hepatocellular carcinoma, but early newborn detection with nitisinone and dietary therapy markedly improves survival and reduces cancer risk; lifelong monitoring remains essential.
pitfalls: Relying on plasma tyrosine alone, which is non-specific, rather than measuring succinylacetone
Attributing infantile liver failure to infection or sepsis and missing the treatable metabolic cause
Assuming nitisinone eliminates hepatocellular carcinoma risk and stopping surveillance
Neglecting phenylalanine and tyrosine dietary control while on nitisinone, risking corneal and skin complications
